label: L3
title: Agents: An Agent Is a Prompt in a Loop
brief: Lecture 3 opens with output contracts. A complaint router that asks for a team in free text and extracts bolded phrases with a regex found a team on 178 of 200 complaints (64% accuracy) and collapsed when the model changed (gpt-4o: 1 of 100 parsed), whereas schema forcing through response_format parsed 100 of 100 for every model with 69–74% accuracy. The model only ever sees one flat token sequence, so it honors the schema because post-training included (instruction + schema → conforming answer) pairs: when that shape appears in context, filling it in is the continuation that scores well. An agent is an LLM plus tools plus the ability to break a task into sub-tasks and execute each with the right tool. Mechanically, the LLM emits a structured request, our ordinary Python code routes it to an external system, wraps the result in a new prompt and calls the LLM again, repeating until a final answer: an agent is a prompt in a loop. Tool use is just generating a function call reliably (schema enforcement again), the tools are described to the model in the prompt, and task decomposition, which once needed brittle ReAct-style prompting, is now largely built into the models.
kp: Free-text output + regex parsing is brittle: the bold-text parser found a team on 178/200 complaints, 64% accuracy.
A model change changes the answer style, which breaks the pattern: gpt-4o-mini 88/100 found (60%), gpt-4.1-mini 78/100 (52%), gpt-4o 1/100 (0%).
Schema forcing (response_format with type json_schema) parsed 100/100 on all three models, accuracy 69–74%.
The API flattens messages + schema into one token string; the model never sees a list, dict or schema object.
The model sticks to the schema because post-training fine-tuned it, by next-word prediction, on (instruction + schema → conforming answer) pairs.
Agent = LLM + tools + the ability to break a task into sub-tasks and execute each with the right tool.
Loop: LLM emits a request → our code routes it to an external system → the result becomes the next prompt → LLM continues, until a final answer.
The orchestration is ordinary Python that we write; the LLM never calls the external system itself.
Using a tool = generating a function call, e.g. get_weather(latitude=42.3736, longitude=-71.1097); tools are described to the LLM in the prompt.
Agent = prompt in a loop; its power comes from tools (data access, code execution, other 'executive' powers). Decomposition once needed brittle ReAct-style prompting.

topics.n: Output contracts: parsing vs schema forcing
topics.x: The complaint router needs exactly one team name. Asked in free text, the model answers in prose with the team bolded inside a sentence, so a regex parser is needed; it found a team on 178/200 complaints with 64% accuracy and fell apart when the model changed. Schema forcing passes a JSON schema through response_format and gave 100% parseable output on every model tested.

The API turns the messages and the schema into one flat token sequence, and the model emits one token at a time; it never sees a dict or a schema. It conforms because post-training repeated Step 1 (fine-tuning by next-word prediction) on instruction + schema → conforming answer pairs, so when that shape appears in context, the continuation that scores well is one that fills it in.

topics.n: What makes an LLM an agent
topics.x: A bare LLM answers from its training data and can be confidently wrong (it described Moo Deng, a pygmy hippo born in July 2024, as a social media influencer). Adding tools such as web search, a calendar, a Python interpreter or email is not enough by itself; an agent also needs the ability to break a task into sub-tasks and execute each with the right tool.

The LLM decides which tool to use and emits a text request; our code routes it to the right external system; the system returns a result; our code builds a second prompt from it and calls the LLM again, which either issues another request or gives the final answer. In the email example the request is a structured email, the result is status code 200, and the second prompt says the email was sent. All of this orchestration is ordinary Python.

Using a tool means generating code that calls a function, such as search_google('2026 FIFA World Cup final winner') or calculate(23833 * 47374). That call must be generated reliably, so the LLM response is schema-enforced just like the router. The LLM knows which tools exist and what they do because we describe them in the prompt; under the hood the whole schematic is one prompt in a loop.

Breaking a task into sub-tasks and using the right tools used to require careful, brittle prompting and harnesses (ReAct, arXiv 2210.03629); modern models handle it. Key ideas: an agent is an LLM in a loop, and its power comes from tools: access to data, access to a code execution environment, and other 'executive' powers.

cards.f: Why does asking the router for a team in free text create a problem?
cards.b: The model answers in prose (e.g. '…should be handled by the **credit reporting** team…' plus a justification), so code has to dig the team out of the text.
cards.x: No output contract means you need a parser.

cards.f: Bold-text regex parser on 200 complaints: results?
cards.x: 22 complaints got no routing at all before accuracy is even considered.

cards.f: Same prompt and parser, three models: results?
cards.x: Model change → style change → pattern change.

cards.f: Schema forcing results across the three models?
cards.x: Schema forcing fixes parseability, not correctness.

cards.f: How is schema forcing requested in code?
cards.b: Send the messages with response_format = {'type': 'json_schema', 'json_schema': SCHEMA}.
cards.x: The lecture's schema has a 'reasoning' string and a 'team' enum.

cards.f: What does the model actually see under schema forcing?
cards.b: One flat token sequence (chat markup + prompt + schema as text). It emits one token at a time and never sees a list, a dict or a schema.
cards.x: The structure lives in your code and the API, not in the model.

cards.f: Why does the LLM stick to the schema?
cards.b: Post-training: fine-tuning by next-word prediction on (instruction + schema → conforming answer) pairs teaches that when this shape is in context, filling it in is the continuation that scores well.
cards.x: It is Step 1 of post-training again; only the answer column changed.

cards.b: Humans wrote high-quality answers to instructions: about 12,500 instruction-answer pairs.
cards.x: This step turns a text continuer into an instruction follower.

cards.f: What makes an LLM an agent?
cards.b: LLM + tools + the ability to break a task into sub-tasks and execute each sub-task using the right tools.
cards.x: Tools alone are not enough: the slide before ends with 'LLM + Tools = Agent?'.

cards.f: The agent loop, step by step
cards.b: Initial prompt → LLM emits a request → our code routes it to an external system → result → our code builds the next prompt → LLM → … → final answer.
cards.x: The LLM never touches the external system directly.

cards.f: Email example: what does each stage produce?
cards.b: LLM: an email request {to, from, subject, body}. Email sender: status code 200. Our code: second prompt 'Email sent successfully'. LLM: 'I have sent the email to Anna as you requested.'
cards.x: The status code is turned into text before the LLM sees it.

cards.b: We do, with ordinary Python code.
cards.x: The lecture builds an agent from scratch in simple Python.

cards.f: What does 'using a tool' mean for an LLM?
cards.b: Generating code that calls a function, e.g. get_weather(latitude=42.3736, longitude=-71.1097) or calculate(23833 * 47374).
cards.x: The hard part is generating that call reliably, hence schema enforcement.

cards.f: How does the LLM know which tools exist and what they do?
cards.b: We tell it in the prompt.
cards.x: Tool descriptions are just more context.

cards.b: A prompt in a loop: the request/route/result/prompt schematic is just an LLM called repeatedly.
cards.x: Its power comes from tools: data access, code execution, other 'executive' powers.

cards.f: Historical note: what used to need careful prompting or harnesses?
cards.b: Getting the model to break a task into sub-tasks and execute each with the right tools (e.g. ReAct, arXiv 2210.03629).
cards.x: 'This used to require careful / brittle prompting… Not anymore.'

quiz.q: Asked 'Which team should handle this complaint?' with the teams listed in plain words, what did the model return?
o: A prose explanation with the team name bolded inside a sentence
Exactly one team code, e.g. CREDIT_REPORTING
A JSON object with 'reasoning' and 'team' fields
A refusal to choose
quiz.e: The model replied '…should be handled by the **credit reporting** team…' and then justified it. A bare code is what the original router prompt demanded, and JSON needs schema forcing.

quiz.q: A bold-text regex parser found a team on 178 of 200 complaints, with 64.0% accuracy measured over all 200. Roughly what share of the complaints where it found a team were routed correctly?
o: About 57%
quiz.e: 64% of 200 = 128 correct, and every correct routing is among the 178 parsed, so 128/178 ≈ 72%. 64% counts the 22 unparsed complaints as wrong; 89% is the parse rate, not accuracy.

quiz.q: Same prompt and same bold-text parser, but the model is switched to gpt-4o. What happened?
o: A team was found on only 1 of 100 complaints, 0% accuracy
100/100 parsed with 74% accuracy
88/100 found with 60% accuracy
Results matched gpt-4o-mini because the prompt did not change
quiz.e: gpt-4o's answer style no longer matched the bold-text pattern. 100/100 at 74% is gpt-4o with schema forcing; 88/100 at 60% is gpt-4o-mini with the parser.

quiz.q: Why does the lecture call parsing free-text LLM output for patterns 'fundamentally non-robust'?
o: A model change changes the answer style, which changes the pattern you must look for
Regular expressions cannot match markdown bold markers
LLMs are trained never to bold text
Parsing is too slow at scale
quiz.e: The slide's chain is: change in model > change in style of answer > change in pattern to look for. The regex did match bold text; the problem is that the style it relied on is not stable.

quiz.q: With the regex parser, gpt-4.1-mini found a team on 78/100 complaints at 52% accuracy; with schema forcing it parsed 100/100 at 69% accuracy. How many more complaints (of 100) were routed correctly with schema forcing?
quiz.e: 69 − 52 = 17 more correct routings. 22 (= 100 − 78) is the gain in parsed outputs, not in correct ones; parseability and accuracy are different measures.

quiz.q: Under schema forcing, what does the model actually receive?
o: One flat token sequence containing the prompt and the schema as text
A Python dict with the schema attached as metadata
Only the prompt; the API checks the schema after generation
A message list plus a schema object it parses natively
quiz.e: The API renders messages and schema into one flat string; the model emits one token at a time and 'never sees a list, a dict, or a schema'. The schema is in the input text, not checked only afterwards.

quiz.q: The model never sees a dict or a schema object. Why, according to the lecture, does it still reliably fill in the schema?
o: Post-training on instruction + schema → conforming-answer pairs taught it that filling in that shape is the continuation that scores well
The schema arrives through a separate structured channel the model reads natively
A reward model scores each output at inference time and rejects non-JSON
The API silently appends few-shot JSON examples to every prompt
quiz.e: The lecture builds (instruction + schema → conforming answer) pairs and fine-tunes by next-word prediction. The schema arrives as plain tokens in one flat string, so there is no structured channel, and the lecture's explanation is training, not an inference-time filter.

quiz.q: In the schema-forcing version of post-training Step 1, what changes relative to the original instruction-answer pairs?
o: The schema becomes part of the input and the target is a schema-conforming answer; training is still next-word prediction
Humans rank JSON outputs and a reward model is trained on the rankings
The model gets a dedicated JSON output head
Only the instruction changes; the target stays a prose answer
quiz.e: 'Step 1 again — only the answer column has changed', with the schema included in the input. Ranking outputs to train a reward model is the RLHF step, not this one.

quiz.q: Per the lecture, what makes an LLM an agent?
o: LLM + tools + the ability to break a task into sub-tasks and execute each with the right tool
An LLM connected to tools such as web search and email
An LLM with retrieval-augmented generation
An LLM post-trained with RLHF
quiz.e: The tools-only version is posed as a question ('LLM + Tools = Agent?'); the definition adds task decomposition and execution with the right tools.

quiz.q: In the basic agent loop, what sends the LLM's request to the external system?
o: Code we write that routes the request
The LLM calls the system's API itself
The external system reads the LLM's output stream
The model provider's servers
quiz.e: 'We write code to route the request to the appropriate external system', and the whole orchestration is ordinary Python. The LLM only generates text.

quiz.q: An agent needs three sequential tool calls before it can answer. Following the lecture's loop, how many times is the LLM called?
quiz.e: Each tool call is triggered by one LLM call, and one more LLM call turns the last result into the final answer: k tool calls → k + 1 LLM calls (the slide shows 2 tool calls and 3 prompts). 3 forgets the final call.

quiz.q: User: 'Email Anna and ask if we can move today's meeting to Monday 11am.' What is the LLM's first output?
o: A structured email request with to, from, subject and body
'I have sent the email to Anna as you requested.'
Status code 200
A web search for Anna's address
quiz.e: The LLM creates a request that can be sent to an email-sending system. 'I have sent the email…' is the final answer after the second prompt, and 200 is the email system's result.

quiz.q: The email-sending system returns status code 200. What happens next?
o: Our code turns it into a second prompt ('Email sent successfully') and the LLM writes the final answer
The status code is shown to the user as the answer
The LLM polls the email system until it sees 200
The loop restarts from the original prompt
quiz.e: Our code converts the status code into the second prompt; the LLM then generates 'I have sent the email to Anna as you requested.' Nothing goes to the user until the LLM's final answer.

quiz.q: In the lecture's schematic, when does the loop stop?
o: When the LLM returns a final answer instead of another tool request
After a fixed number of iterations set by the API
When an external system returns status code 200
When the schema check fails
quiz.e: Each LLM output is either a request to route or the final answer. A 200 is just a tool result that becomes the next prompt.

quiz.q: For an LLM, what does 'using a tool' mean?
o: Generating code that calls a function, e.g. get_weather(latitude=42.3736, longitude=-71.1097)
Running the function inside the model's weights
Retrieving documents and pasting them into the prompt
Fine-tuning on the tool's documentation
quiz.e: Using a tool = generating code that calls a function. Executing it is our code's job, and pasting retrieved documents is RAG.

quiz.q: How does the LLM learn which external tools are available and what they do?
o: We describe them in the prompt
Each tool is fine-tuned into the model
It infers them from the API key
It searches the web for tool documentation
quiz.e: 'By telling it in the prompt!!' Tool descriptions are context, not training.

quiz.q: Why does the lecture describe tool calling as 'output contracts, again'?
o: The LLM must emit a function call our code can parse and route every time, so its response is schema-enforced like the router's JSON
Tools return JSON that the LLM must validate before answering
Each tool must be fine-tuned into the model with its own contract
The final answer to the user must always be JSON
quiz.e: The tool-call slide says 'Schema enforcement for the LLM response, just like our router.' The contract governs the LLM's request, not the tool's output or the final answer.

quiz.q: Per the historical note, what used to require careful, brittle prompting and harnesses (e.g. ReAct) but largely no longer does?
o: Getting the model to break a task into sub-tasks and execute each with the right tool
Producing JSON that matches a schema
Describing the available tools to the model
Routing requests to external systems
quiz.e: Decomposition 'used to require careful / brittle prompting… Not anymore.' Tools are still described in the prompt, and routing is still our code's job.

written.q: A team routes consumer-finance complaints with an LLM. Compare (a) asking for the team in free text and extracting it with a regex and (b) schema forcing. Use the lecture's numbers, explain what the model actually receives under schema forcing, why it nonetheless conforms, and what schema forcing does and does not fix.
written.m: (a) In free text the model answers in prose, e.g. bolding '**credit reporting**' inside a sentence, so a regex parser is needed. On 200 complaints it found a team on 178 with 64% accuracy. The parser is tied to one model's style: with the same prompt, gpt-4o-mini found 88/100 (60%), gpt-4.1-mini 78/100 (52%) and gpt-4o 1/100 (0%). A model change changes the style, which changes the pattern, so pattern parsing is fundamentally non-robust. (b) Schema forcing sends response_format = {type: json_schema, json_schema: SCHEMA}, with fields such as reasoning and an enum of teams. Every model then gave 100/100 parseable outputs, with 70%, 69% and 74% accuracy. The API flattens messages and schema into one token string; the model emits one token at a time and never sees a dict or a schema. It conforms because post-training repeated Step 1 (supervised fine-tuning by next-word prediction) on instruction + schema → conforming answer pairs, so when that shape appears in context, filling it in is the continuation that scores well. Schema forcing guarantees the output contract (parseable output, a valid team) but not correctness: accuracy stays around 70%.
k: Free-text prose forces a regex/bold parser
Model swap breaks the parser; gpt-4o 1/100, 0%
Schema forcing via response_format json_schema: 100/100 parsed, 69–74% accuracy
Model sees one flat token sequence, no structured schema
Conformity explained by post-training on instruction + schema → conforming-answer pairs

written.q: Explain how an LLM becomes an agent. Define an agent as the lecture does, walk through the loop for 'Email Anna and ask if we can move today's meeting to Monday 11am', separate what the LLM does from what our code does, explain how the LLM knows the tools and how tool calls are made reliable, and state how many LLM calls a task with k sequential tool calls needs.
written.m: Agent = LLM + tools (web search, calendar, Python interpreter, email…) + the ability to break a task into sub-tasks and execute each with the right tool. Loop: the initial prompt goes to the LLM, which picks the email tool and emits a structured request {to: anna@…, from, subject, body}. Our code recognizes an email request and routes it to the email sender rather than web search or the calculator. The sender returns status code 200; our code converts it into a second prompt ('Email sent successfully'), and the LLM writes the final answer 'I have sent the email to Anna as you requested.' The LLM only generates text (requests and the final answer); ordinary Python written by us routes requests, calls external systems and builds each new prompt. Tool use is generating a function call, made reliable by schema enforcement as in the router, and the tools are described to the LLM in the prompt. Complex tasks repeat the cycle: k sequential tool calls need k + 1 LLM calls, the last producing the final answer. So an agent is a prompt in a loop, and its power comes from tools: data, code execution and other executive powers.
k: LLM emits a structured request, not the action itself
Our Python code routes, calls the system, builds the next prompt
Status code 200 → second prompt → final answer
Tools described in the prompt; tool calls schema-enforced
k tool calls → k + 1 LLM calls
Agent = prompt in a loop; power from tools
